title: Dedication
hookLine: giving away the merit of every practice to all beings

cards: Someone has spent an afternoon copying a sutra by hand, line after careful line, the ink still drying. Whatever good came from it, it's theirs. They earned it.

And then, before the brush is washed, they give it away. In Mahayana practice, the last words of a session can be words that aren't about the one who practiced at all. They send the good of it out the door, to everyone.

teach.h: MERIT: THE FRUIT OF A GOOD ACT.
teach.b: Year one met this as sharing the merit; today, the Mahayana turn on it. First, the thing given. Buddhists speak of merit, punya in Sanskrit, puñña in Pali: the good that comes from a good act.

Giving, keeping a precept, sitting, chanting, each leaves something behind, like warmth in a room after a fire. The old teaching says good acts bear good fruit; merit is that fruit while it ripens. Second, the turn.
In Mahayana practice, merit isn't kept.
At the close of a sit or a ceremony, people recite a dedication, turning the merit toward the awakening of all beings. The Sanskrit word is parinamana, often given in English as turning over.

The bodhisattva works for all, so even the fruit of the work goes to all. Shantideva's Way of the Bodhisattva closes with a whole chapter of it: may the good of this go here, and there, and to every being in pain.
Third, a neighbor in the same house. Theravada Buddhists share merit too.

After a meal offered to monks, or a chant for someone who has died, a family may pour water slowly from one vessel into another while the monks recite verses, and the merit is shared with the dead and with all beings.
Different words, the same open hand. Fourth, the strange arithmetic. Isn't merit given away lost?
Some teachers in this tradition say the opposite: a lamp that lights another lamp isn't dimmed.
Either way, the practice ends the session facing outward. The last thought isn't how did I do. It's who else is this for.

how: Mahayana communities close a sit, chant or ceremony with a dedication of merit to all beings; in Theravada communities merit is shared too, sometimes while water is poured from one vessel into another as monks recite verses.

games.q: you've just finished a long sit and it went well. the session isn't over yet. what comes last?
o: turn its good toward all beings
set a longer goal for tomorrow
games.why: in Mahayana practice the last words dedicate the merit to all beings, so the session ends facing outward.

practice: Sit for a little while, the way you have on other days, nothing special.
Near the end, think of whatever steadiness or quiet this sit gave you, even a little, and send it out: to someone you love, to someone you don't know, to someone having a harder day than you.
If you have words from your own tradition for this, say them; if not, the intention is enough.

wordCard.voice: Dedication. Parinamana, turning the merit of a practice toward all beings, so the good of it doesn't stay with the one who did it. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: turning over, the dedication of merit to others.

carryVoice: Your line: given away. The good goes out the door, to everyone. See you tomorrow.
